doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Demonstrating mutes
summary: He demonstrates open horn, Harmon, plunger and cup mutes and what each does.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: I love what the mutes can do for an instrument. Do you mind showing me a little bit of that?
What, would you like to hear what the different —
I’d like to hear what they do.

Well the mutes, okay, I love working with mutes because it can change the texture of what you’re playing. All right open horn. [audio] Make it ring, all right, okay. So then you take a Harmon mute and you take the stem out and you get close to the microphone and you approximately what Miles [audio] or you can put the stem in and you can sound like some of the Duke Ellington trumpet sections. [audio] really an intense, black, Harlem feel. [audio] the wa-wa, okay. And then you have the good old plunger, which of course again is more traditional, Muggsy Spanier [audio]. You can get that feel too, but [audio] all you’re doing is altering the flow of air there.
Available at your local hardware store, right?

And this is a Denis Wick, a British manufacturer, a plastic mute and it’s very versatile in that it can become a cup mute [audio] which blends very well with a nice, soft sax, or if you want an intensity for duets with a clarinet, and I’m talking about the timbre of the,
okay, now if I get in a hot duet with somebody playing “China Boy” like on the clarinet [audio] I’m not going to overblow the clarinet.
I love that cup mute. It has such as sound reminiscent of, I don’t know, it speaks of a certain era almost.
Oh it’s mellow. [audio] It’s very intimate for ballad playing. So here I’ve got one-two- three-four-five-six, six different combinations depending on what I want to make that song do.
I’m jealous as a saxophone player you know.
